tour.title: Kathmandu: Gods, Kings and Living Goddesses
tour.summary: A living goddess, Malla kings, hippie lanes and market squares — ending with the 365-step climb to the all-seeing eyes of Swayambhunath.
tour.overviewText:
Listen. That low ringing you hear is three religions sharing one bell.

You are standing in the old heart of Kathmandu, capital of Nepal, a bowl-shaped valley city of well over a million people where motorbikes, pigeons, marigold sellers and office workers all squeeze through the same medieval lanes. The people whose city this really is are the Newar, the valley's original inhabitants, farmers and traders and craftsmen who built these brick courtyards and carved every window you are about to see. Daily life here does not pause for sacredness. A woman lights a butter lamp, a boy kicks a football past a shrine, a shopkeeper weighs brass bells. Sacred and ordinary sit on top of each other.

And here is the thing that makes Kathmandu matter, the idea that unlocks the whole walk: Hindus and Buddhists here do not really choose sides. The same god gets a Hindu name in one shrine and a Buddhist name in the next, and nobody thinks that is strange. You will meet the Malla kings, the medieval Newar rulers who ran these city-states from about 1200 to 1768 and turned rivalry into architecture, each king adding a temple to outshine the last. You will meet the Kumari, a prepubescent girl worshipped as the living vessel of the goddess Taleju, who lives cloistered until puberty retires her. You will walk a Durbar Square, durbar just means royal palace, so this is literally palace-square, the stage where kings were crowned and gods are still paraded. And you will end at a stupa, a domed Buddhist shrine holding relics, its four pairs of eyes watching the valley.

Why does that mix survive? Partly because it works, and partly because it broke. The 2015 earthquake killed thousands across Nepal and flattened whole streets here. What you see today is a city mid-repair: some temples rebuilt timber by timber, some still braced with scaffolding and struts. The cracks are part of the story, not a footnote.

The shape of the walk is simple. You start flat, in the palace squares and market lanes of the old town, then you head west out of the bazaar and finish with a real climb, 365 steep stone steps up Swayambhu hill to the great white stupa above the haze.

Practicals. The route is about 4 km of walking plus the hill climb, and you want most of a morning for it. Start around 8:30 to 9, when the light is clean and the squares are waking up. The Durbar Square area asks foreign visitors for around Rs 1,000, rupees, Nepali rupees, and Swayambhu asks around Rs 200 at the stairway base; both change, so verify at the gate and carry small cash. Wear shoes you can slip off, because you will be asked to leave them outside shrines. Walk clockwise around stupas and shrines, that is the respectful direction, keeping the holy thing to your right, and carry water for the hill. There is no shade on those steps.

Come curious, walk gently, and let the city do the talking.
tour.difficulty: Easy and flat through Durbar Square and the market lanes, then a real climb: 365 steep stone steps up Swayambhu hill with no shade. Take it slowly and carry water.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 8:30 to 9am, so you reach Swayambhu before the midday haze and heat. Mornings are also when the Kumari sometimes appears at her window, and the light on the stupa's eyes is at its best.
tour.imageCredits: Photographs are bundled from Wikimedia Commons under public domain or Creative Commons licences. Full attribution for each image appears on its stop page and in Settings.

stops.name: Kumari Ghar, House of the Living Goddess
stops.narration:
Stop in front of the whitewashed house with the carved wooden windows and the lions at the door. You are looking at a goddess's house, and she is home.

Inside lives the Kumari, a prepubescent girl worshipped as the living vessel of Taleju, a fierce protective goddess once adopted as the patron of the Malla kings, those medieval Newar rulers who built this square. The selection is brutally specific: the girl must be from a certain Newar Buddhist clan, show no blemish or lost tooth, and pass secret ritual tests. Once chosen, she moves in here, wears red and gold, receives devotees with a glance, a nod is said to bless, tears to warn, and leaves only for festivals. At puberty, the goddess is understood to depart, the girl retires with a pension, and the priests find the next vessel. It is devotion and a stolen childhood in the same room, and honest guides say both halves out loud.

She sometimes appears at the central window in the morning, no schedule, no tickets, no elbowing. If the curtain moves, be still and be lucky. And here is the hard rule, stated plainly: never photograph HER. Photographing the Kumari herself is forbidden and deeply disrespectful. Courtyard exterior only, and put the camera down entirely if she appears.

The courtyard is free to enter in daylight hours, covered by the general Durbar Square area, verify locally, since rules shift. Step inside, look up at the carved windows, and keep your voice low. Families bring sick babies here. Tourists bring curiosity. Both are allowed, but only one of them matters.

What you just learned is the engine of this whole walk: in Kathmandu, a god can be a neighbour.
stops.entranceFeeNote: The courtyard is free to enter during the day. Entry is covered by the general Durbar Square area; no separate Kumari ticket. Verify locally.
stops.openingHours: Courtyard generally open in daylight hours. The Kumari appears at the window unpredictably, most reliably in the morning and during festivals such as Indra Jatra.
stops.accessibility: Step-free into the courtyard from the lane, but the surface is old brick and uneven. The upper floors are not open to visitors.
stops.insiderTip: Come back during Indra Jatra in September if you can: the Kumari is paraded in a chariot right past this door, and the whole square turns into the biggest party of the Nepali year.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the courtyard and walk north across the square, past the statue on the tall pillar, towards the palace wing with the Hanuman statue beside its gate. That is Hanuman Dhoka, about a minute away.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sundar1, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Hanuman Dhoka Palace
stops.narration:
Turn toward the long palace wing with the monkey god standing guard by its gate. That is Hanuman Dhoka, dhoka means gate, and Hanuman is the Hindu monkey god of loyalty and strength, which is why a king would want him on the door. This whole sprawling complex is the old royal palace of the Malla kings, those medieval Newar rulers who competed in architecture the way modern cities compete in stadiums.

Walk in, your Durbar Square ticket, around Rs 1,000 for foreign visitors, verify at the gate, covers these museum courtyards, and you are walking through three centuries of throne rooms at once. The courtyards stack styles: carved wooden windows from the Malla centuries, white plaster arcades added by later Shah and Rana rulers, new timber standing next to earthquake-braced walls. Kings were crowned in the inner Nasal Chowk courtyard right into modern times; Nepal stayed a monarchy until 2008, which is within plenty of your guides' lifetimes.

What you are learning here is how Nepali power worked: not by clearing the old, but by adding. Each dynasty built beside the last instead of knocking it down, so the palace reads like a pile of love letters from rival kings.

Two practical things. First, the tall nine-storey tower involves brutally steep ladders, skip it if your knees object; the courtyards are the point. Second, the 2015 earthquake tore through here. Some of what you see is restored, some is still propped and patched. Do not read the scaffolding as failure. In a living palace, repair is the tradition.

Take the museum slowly, then step back into the sun. The square's biggest temple is waiting across the bricks.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign visitors pay around Rs 1,000 for the Durbar Square ticket, which covers the palace museum courtyards. SAARC nationals pay less. Prices change, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Palace museum roughly 09:00 to 17:00 daily. The outer square is open access at all hours.
stops.accessibility: The museum courtyards involve steps, narrow doorways and uneven old stone. The nine-storey tower climb is steep ladders and not for everyone.
stops.insiderTip: The Tribhuvan Museum section inside holds the king's thrones and crown jewels crowds walk straight past — slow down there, it is the quietest room in the palace.
stops.nextStopDirections: Exit the palace gate and walk south-west across the square, past the tall Maju Dega temple on your right, towards the long low restored pavilion at the square's south-west corner. That is Kasthamandap, about two minutes away.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Safalphotos, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kasthamandap Pavilion
stops.narration:
Cross to the long, low, barn-like pavilion at the square's corner. It looks modest next to the gilt temples. It is the reason the city is called Kathmandu.

The name breaks apart: kastha means wood, mandap means pavilion. Legend says this whole three-storey rest house was cut from a single tree, raised as a travellers' shelter on the old Tibet-India trade road. Traders slept here, pilgrims waited out the rain here, and a market town grew around the shelter until the shelter gave the town its name. How many world capitals are named after a hostel? That joke lands on the fact: this was always a city that made money by giving strangers a bed.

Now look closer, because the building is also a document of the 2015 earthquake. The quake flattened it completely, the pavilion collapsed into a pile of carved timber. What you see now is the rebuild, finished timber by timber with traditional joinery, old carvings slotted back where they survived. Nepalese craftsmen argue fiercely about whether reconstructions should look old or admit they are new; here they chose faithful. Run your eye along the struts. New wood sits beside old.

Inside the ground floor sits a small shrine to Gorakhnath, a yogi-saint revered by ascetics, which is why wandering sadhus, Hindu holy men, still gather here. Your Durbar Square ticket covers all this, around Rs 1,000, verify at the gate; there is no separate fee.

What you learned: a city can lose its namesake and rebuild it. That is not nostalgia. That is maintenance.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the Durbar Square foreign-visitor ticket (around Rs 1,000; verify at the gate). No separate fee to walk around and under the pavilion.
stops.openingHours: Open access in daylight hours as part of the square.
stops.accessibility: Level ground around the pavilion with some uneven old paving. The raised plinth has steps and no ramp.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the Gorakhnath shrine inside the pavilion's ground floor — the ascetic god's image is why sadhus still gather here, and it is easy to miss behind the columns.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north-east back towards the centre of the square, about fifty metres, to the tall triple-roofed Vishnu temple with the gilded doorway. That is Trailokya Mohan.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Chainwit., CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Trailokya Mohan Narayan Temple
stops.narration:
Walk fifty metres back toward the centre of the square to the tall temple with the triple roofs and the glowing doorway. This is Trailokya Mohan, a temple to Narayan, that is Vishnu, the Hindu preserver god, under one of his grandest titles: lord of the three worlds.

What you are learning here is small and sharp: how a Newar temple works as a machine. The triple roofs are not decoration; each smaller tier sheds monsoon rain off the carved struts below, and those struts, look up, carry armies of gods and highly uninhibited lovers side by side. The sanctum inside is small, dark and hot with oil lamps, meant for one priest and the god, not a congregation. Worship happens at the threshold: bells, marigolds, a coin, a forehead to the doorframe. The gilded doorway is the interface, and at dusk it catches the last sun and burns gold against the brick. Stand on the Kasthamandap side and wait for it.

A note on manners, because it matters everywhere today: the sanctum is for Hindu worshippers. You admire from outside, shoes off if you step onto the plinth, no peering with a flash. That is not exclusion. That is a god at home.

And here is the overlap lesson again, since Kathmandu will drill it into you: the Buddhist traders who fund this square's shops will stop at this Hindu doorway too, light a lamp, and keep walking. Your Durbar Square ticket covers the exterior, around Rs 1,000, verify at the gate, and the view is free anyway.

Touch nothing gilt, ring nothing without watching a local first, and look down at the paving. Those worn hollows are centuries of foreheads and feet. The temple counts attendance in stone.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the Durbar Square foreign-visitor ticket (around Rs 1,000; verify at the gate). The sanctum is for Hindu worshippers; visitors admire from outside.
stops.openingHours: Exterior visible at all hours; the square is open access. The shrine opens for worship in the morning and evening.
stops.accessibility: Viewed from the level square. The temple plinth itself is stepped with no ramp.
stops.insiderTip: Stand back at the Kasthamandap side at dusk: the gilded doorway catches the last light and the whole temple glows against the darkening brick.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk a few steps north to the biggest triple-roofed temple on the square, rising from a tall nine-stepped platform. That is Maju Dega, right beside you.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sumobie, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Maju Dega Temple
stops.narration:
Now face the biggest thing on the square: the triple-roofed temple towering over you on its stepped pyramid. This is Maju Dega, and your legs are about to learn it.

The facts first. It was built in 1692 by Riddhi Lakshmi, the queen mother of one of those Malla kings, note that, a woman commissioning the square's grandest monument as an act of piety and politics. The base is nine great stepped terraces of brick and stone, rising like a wedding cake, with the little triple-roofed shrine perched on top. Nine is not an accident: stepped platforms lift the god above the dust and lift you, step by panting step, out of the everyday.

So sit. Everyone does. These lower steps are Kathmandu's most democratic bench, porters eating dal bhat, which is the lentil-and-rice staple you will smell all day, students sharing earphones, pigeons negotiating crumbs. The third or fourth level already gives the full panorama, and that is honest advice: the upper tiers are steep, the drops are real, and there are no rails. Climb only as high as feels safe.

What you are learning up here is urbanism. From even halfway up, the square resolves into a machine: palace on one side for power, temples in the middle for gods, market lanes radiating outward for money. The Malla kings designed that on purpose. A Durbar Square is not a decoration. It is a throne with a view of its own legitimacy.

Look west while you rest. On a clear morning you can pick out the white dome on its hill, Swayambhu, where this walk ends. Enjoy sitting. The lane to Freak Street drops off just south of here.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Covered by the Durbar Square foreign-visitor ticket (around Rs 1,000; verify at the gate). Sitting on the lower steps is free and expected.
stops.openingHours: Exterior and steps accessible at all hours within the square.
stops.accessibility: The platform is nine steep stepped tiers with no handrail or ramp. The square around it is level but cobbled and uneven.
stops.insiderTip: Climb only as high as feels safe — the upper tiers are steep with big drops and no rails. The third or fourth level already gives the full panorama.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south out of the square, past the Kumari Ghar corner, and follow the lane downhill for about two minutes into the narrow street of old guesthouses and guitar shops. That is Freak Street, old Jhochhen.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Jan Kranendonk, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Freak Street (Jhochhen)
stops.narration:
Now turn downhill into the narrow lane with the guitar shops and the smell of frying momos, dumplings, you will smell them everywhere today. This is Jhochhen, which the world knows as Freak Street.

Here is the mechanism, and it is pure economics. In the 1960s and 70s, the overland hippie trail ran from Istanbul to Delhi to Kathmandu, and this lane, cheap guesthouses two minutes from Durbar Square, became its terminus. Hashish was effectively legal in Nepal until 1973, and licensed shops sold it over the counter. Long-haired kids who had ridden buses for six weeks could sleep for pennies, eat a banana pancake, buy a handmade guitar and mail a letter home saying they had found enlightenment. Then the licences closed, the scene tightened, and the circus moved to Thamel, the tourist district north of here.

What you are learning is how a street remembers a party it did not quite get invited to. The old-timers will tell you every rock star came here. Most did not, at least not as residents, and that is the joke that lands on the fact: Freak Street's fame outgrew its guest list. What was real was the exchange. Nepali merchants learned English and rock chords; travellers learned that a thangka, a Tibetan Buddhist scroll painting, is not a poster but a meditation diagram, every colour and gesture coded.

So browse. If a thangka seller offers to unroll one, say yes and listen, that is a free lesson in Buddhist iconography. Buy tea, not tall tales. And notice the buildings themselves: carved Newar windows above trekking-gear signs, because the hippies left but the craftsmen stayed.
stops.entranceFeeNote: A public lane. Your only expense will be tea and whatever the guitar shops talk you into.
stops.openingHours: Always open as a street. Shops roughly 09:00 to 20:00; rooftops serve until late evening.
stops.accessibility: A narrow lane with uneven paving and occasional motorbikes threading through. Step-free along its length but crowded.
stops.insiderTip: The thangka painting shops here will unroll anything if you ask — even if you are not buying, watching a master explain the iconography is a free masterclass.
stops.nextStopDirections: Head back north to the square's south edge, then walk north-west through the bazaar lanes for about five minutes, following signs for Indra Chowk. The big open market square with the temple on its platform is your next stop.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Holynow, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Indra Chowk and Akash Bhairav
stops.narration:
Follow the smell of incense and diesel into the wide market square. This is Indra Chowk, and it is Kathmandu's living room and cash register in one.

The temple on the platform with the huge silver face is Akash Bhairav, Bhairav means a fierce, protective form of the god Shiva, and akash means sky, so this is the sky-guardian of the city. His masked face only shows fully during festival week, which tells you something real about how gods work here: they are not always on display. Power is unveiled on schedule.

And the schedule that matters most is Indra Jatra, the September festival named for Indra, king of the Hindu gods and lord of rain. For about a week, this square becomes the centre of Nepal. Masked dancers perform, the living goddess Kumari is paraded in a wooden chariot, and a giant mask of Bhairav is unveiled with straws in its mouth pouring blessed beer and rice wine for anyone holding a cup. It marks the end of the monsoon and honours the dead, grief and harvest party in one week.

But do not wait for September to learn the square's other lesson. Watch the ground floor: bead sellers restringing glass pote necklaces, spice pyramids, brass pots, phone-card stalls. Newar market squares were machines for turning harvests and pilgrimages into money, and they still are. The shrine upstairs and the shop downstairs were never separate businesses.

Walk clockwise around the temple platform if you circle it, shoes off if you step onto shrine stone, and keep to the edges, motorbikes thread this crowd with total confidence and zero brakes.
stops.entranceFeeNote: A public market square. The Akash Bhairav shrine is viewed from outside; leave a small donation if you enter.
stops.openingHours: Market busiest roughly 09:00 to 19:00. The shrine opens for morning and evening worship.
stops.accessibility: Flat but crowded, with uneven paving, open drains at the edges and motorbikes. Not easy with wheels; go slowly.
stops.insiderTip: The bead and pote sellers on the north side will restring a broken necklace while you wait — a classic Indra Chowk errand that costs almost nothing.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk north out of the square along the main lane for about two minutes, following signs for Jana Bahal. Turn into the temple courtyard with the white shrine and the stone water spouts. That is the White Machhendranath temple.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Maesi64, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: White Machhendranath, Jana Bahal
stops.narration:
Duck through the archway into the quiet courtyard and breathe. You just left the loudest square in the city for one of its gentlest. This is Jana Bahal, home of Seto Machhendranath, seto means white.

The white-faced god inside is Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. A bodhisattva is an enlightened being who postpones final escape from suffering to help everyone else out first, and Avalokiteshvara is compassion itself, Hindus worship him too, under the name Machhendranath, as a bringer of rain. One god, two religions, zero argument. If Kathmandu's Hindu-Buddhist overlap had a headquarters, you are standing in it.

Here is the mechanism you can actually see. Look for the massive stacked timbers stored around the courtyard, some as long as a bus. Every spring, in a festival that follows the lunar calendar so its dates shift year to year, those timbers become a towering chariot, the god is lifted aboard, and neighbourhoods haul him through the old town for days. Wheels break. Ropes snap. Everyone heaves together anyway. The festival is engineering, devotion and traffic jam in equal parts, and it ends with the god back home until next year.

Now find the stone water spouts along the wall, the jahru, carved conduits fed by old underground channels that once watered the whole city. People still fill jars here, wash their faces, water the shrine. Before pipes, this was infrastructure as sacred architecture.

Walk clockwise, speak low, leave a small donation if you enter the sanctum. Morning is when the lamps are fresh and the courtyard belongs to the locals.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free courtyard. A small donation at the shrine is customary but not required.
stops.openingHours: Courtyard open in daylight hours. Morning worship is the liveliest time.
stops.accessibility: Level courtyard reached through an archway with a small step. The water-spout area can be wet and slippery.
stops.insiderTip: If the chariot timbers are stored here, ask a local which month the Jatra falls this year — the date follows the lunar calendar and shifts annually.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the courtyard and walk west along the Chhetrapati road for about twenty minutes, following signs for Swayambhu. Pass Chhetrapati Chowk, keep to the main road as it bends, and stop at the small tantric temple complex just before the hill rises. That is Bijeshwari.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Rajesh Dhungana, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Bijeshwari (Bajra Yogini) Temple
stops.narration:
You needed this pause, and the city knew it.

Step off the main road into this compound and the traffic falls away. This is Bijeshwari, a temple to Bajra Yogini, yogini means a powerful female tantric deity, and tantra here means a hands-on, esoteric strand of Hindu-Buddhist practice with mantras and offerings. You do not need to master the theology. Watch what people do: ring the bell, leave a marigold, tip a little oil into a lamp, touch their forehead to the threshold. The mechanism is transaction and tenderness at once, feed the goddess, and she feeds you back.

What you are learning here is scale. After the palace squares, with their royal bombast, this is religion at neighbourhood size. Old men gossip on the steps. Kids chase each other around the shrines. The priests know everyone's name. This is what most Kathmandu worship actually looks like, not festivals with chariots, but Tuesday mornings with a bag of rice and a prayer squeezed in before work.

Look around the compound before you leave. The smaller shrines crowded into the corners are classic Kathmandu: Hindu gods and Buddhist figures sharing one courtyard wall, because the priests of one tradition will happily tend the gods of the other. Nobody here is guarding a border between faiths.

Take your shoes off where asked, step over thresholds rather than on them, and leave a few rupees for oil if you light a lamp. Then drink your water. The hill is waiting, and the 365 steps start just past this lane.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter the compound. Small donations for butter lamps are customary.
stops.openingHours: Open daylight hours, liveliest in the morning and around sunset prayers.
stops.accessibility: Level compound with some steps at individual shrines. Fully step-free routes are limited.
stops.insiderTip: The small shops on the lane outside sell the best pre-climb provisions: roasted peanuts, water, and kukri-shaped souvenirs you absolutely do not need.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk west to the base of the hill and find the great eastern stairway with the Buddha statues flanking its foot. Climb all 365 steps to the top — slowly, with rests at the landings. The stupa waits at the summit.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Sangita21957, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Swayambhunath Stupa
stops.narration:
You climbed 365 steps. Earn the view before you earn the meaning.

Turn around slowly. The whole Kathmandu bowl spreads below you, brick cubes, temple roofs, rice fields at the edges, haze doing its best to hide the Himalaya. You are higher than every palace you walked through, which is exactly the point. Faith up here outranks power down there.

Now face the stupa, that great white dome with the gilded cube and the four pairs of painted eyes staring down each compass direction. A stupa is a domed Buddhist shrine, part reliquary and part diagram of the universe, its eyes the all-seeing awareness of the Buddha. This one is old, something like fifteen centuries of rebuilding and regilding on this hilltop, and it belongs to everyone. Buddhists circle it spinning prayer wheels, Hindus offer to the goddess Harati at her temple on the same terrace, monkeys beg and steal around the edges, which is why visitors call this the Monkey Temple. Hold your snacks like money.

Walk clockwise, keeping the dome to your right, and spin the wheels the same direction. Shoes off where asked, especially at Harati's temple, she is the protector of children, once a child-eater converted by the Buddha. Kathmandu reforms its gods instead of firing them.

The 2015 quake cracked shrines up here and toppled small chapels; the big dome held. What you see is patched, regilded, alive.

You paid around Rs 200 at the stairway base, verify at the gate, prices move. Sit on the eastern edge and watch the city you just crossed. This is the end of the walk: palace to market to hilltop, power to money to prayer. Descend by the steps or the gentler west road. Taxis wait below..
stops.entranceFeeNote: Foreign visitors pay around Rs 200 at the ticket counter near the eastern stairway base. SAARC nationals pay less. Prices change, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Hilltop open roughly sunrise to sunset, around 05:00 to 19:00. Come early or late for the best light and fewest monkeys with attitude.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible: 365 steep stone steps with no lift, plus uneven paving and slopes at the summit. There is a longer vehicle road up the west side that avoids the steps but still involves slopes.
stops.insiderTip: For sunset, arrive at least an hour early and claim an eastern-edge spot — the sun drops behind the hills and the whole stupa turns gold while the city lights come on below.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Descend by the same eastern stairway, or take the western vehicle road down for a gentler slope. Taxis wait near both bases for the ride back to Thamel or Durbar Square.
